items.title: Feeling Tension in the Lower-Body After Your Latest Adventure? Do This Simple Stretch.
items.summary:
I often sing the praises of the Warrior I yoga pose (a.k.a. Virabhadrasana I) to skeptical students who feel that it’s a lot of work without a lot of noticeable benefit, so let me explain my enthusiasm for it.

In my work as a physical therapist and yoga teacher, I’ve noticed that many people in our sedentary society have tight hip flexors, which they don’t stretch much, if at all. I’m convinced that short, tight hip flexors are a major factor in many cases of chronic or recurring back pain that so many people experience in the West.

The hip flexors become tight when the hips are constantly placed in a flexed position—think sitting, driving, or sleeping in the fetal position. Like any other muscles, hip flexors will shorten structurally if they are not stretched. However, if you incorporate Virabhadrasana I or Warrior I into your regular practice, you’ll stretch the hip flexors, helping them gradually return to their normal length and easing a source of backaches.

What Are the Hip Flexors and What Do They Do? 
 The hip flexor muscles include the iliacus, psoas, rectus femoris, tensor fasciae latae, sartorius, and, in some situations, the short adductors pectines and adductor brevis. All of these muscles (except the adductors mentioned) cross the front of the hip and are active in hip flexion, which pulls the femur (thighbone) and torso closer together. The hip flexes when you perform a sit-up or lift your leg toward your chest while standing. (Each of these muscles has other actions, too, but we’re focusing here on their hip-flexing ability.)

items.title: 3 Dead in Plane Crash on Remote North Rim of Grand Canyon National Park
items.summary:
Three people are dead after a plane crashed on the North Rim of Grand Canyon National Park on November 15, 2026.

Authorities have not released the identities of the people aboard the plane or details about the accident. The National Transportation Safety Board is investigating the accident, the National Park Service (NPS) wrote in a statement .

According to the NPS, the Grand Canyon Regional Communications Center received a call about a missing Piper Comanche at 11:30 P.M. on November 15. Produced between 1958 and 1972, the Piper Comanche is an older single-engine, low-wing aircraft that typically seats between four and six people.

The Arizona Department of Public Safety conducted an aerial search in the early morning hours of November 16 using infrared and night vision, according to the NPS.

“The aircraft and debris field were located by NPS at approximately 10:15 A.M. on November 16 in the Basin area,” officials said. “There were no survivors.”

The North Rim is an isolated part of the Grand Canyon that sees just about ten percent of the park’s visitors annually. It’s a rugged, higher-elevation area on the Kaibab Plateau that averages about 8,300 feet—roughly 1,000 feet higher than the South Rim. All park amenities on the North Rim are closed November through April, and the road into the park closes in December.

The Arizona Department of Public Safety, Coconino County Search and Rescue, Kane County Search and Rescue, and Air Force Rescue Coordination Center participated in the search efforts.

items.title: I Took a Mystery “Decision Detox” Trip With Zero Planning. Here’s What Happened.
items.summary:
From the treehouse-like deck outside my hotel room, I took in the lush cluster of live oak and eucalyptus trees all around me, the whisper of wind and chirp of unknown birds, and the small sliver of Pacific Ocean peeking through the foliage-lined horizon. I was completely at peace. The best part: I hadn’t made a single decision for the entire weekend. In fact, until just a couple days prior—the day of my trip departure—I had absolutely no idea where I’d be on this gorgeous Sunday morning.

The morning of my trip, I tore open a sealed envelope that held all the information about the hotel where I’d be staying ( Chaminade Resort and Spa ), my itinerary ( forest therapy , spa treatments, dining at The View and Lago di Como ), and even the destination itself (Santa Cruz, California). This was all part of the “mystery travel” experience I eagerly agreed to, facilitated by Benchmark Resorts & Hotels and Pack Up + Go , an agency that plans completely curated surprise vacations. Here was the deal: I filled out a survey about my preferences (my priorities while traveling, the types of hotels I liked) along with budget, then they planned the entire trip, and I wouldn’t find out details (beyond some notes about weather and packing suggestions) until I opened my envelope the morning of my departure.

The author’s mystery envelope from Pack Up + Go. (Photo: Kristine Thomason)

items.title: Why Your Body Is Begging You to Run More Trails Instead of Roads
items.summary:
Running a marathon beats up your body. Your leg muscles will be damaged on a cellular level, which will translate into soreness and loss of strength that will persist for a week or more. Now imagine how much worse it would be if you were running one of those crazy mountain marathons with rough terrain and steep climbs and descents. It would be awful… right?

Maybe not, according to a new study in Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise led by Mélanie Metra and Guillaume Millet of France’s Université Jean Monnet Saint-Étienne. Millet, who once finished third at the absurdly difficult 200-mile Tor des Géants mountain ultra, is one of the world’s leading trail running researchers. I’ve previously covered his research on the differences between trail and road runners , how to run uphill , how to succeed at Ultra-Trail du Mont-Blanc , and other trail-centric topics.

This time, Millet and his colleagues explore the question of whether road or trail running beats you up more. It’s not a perfect study (for reasons we’ll come back to), but it has some very interesting—and somewhat surprising—insights.

What They Did 
 The researchers asked runners to undertake one of the following three challenges: a simulated road marathon of roughly 26 miles on a treadmill; a simulated trail marathon on a treadmill; or an actual trail marathon on a trail outside the lab.

They took a whole bunch of measures of “neuromuscular fatigue” before and after the marathon, then again one day, two days, and seven days later. These involved various measures of leg strength, maximal jumps,…
items.t: Why Your Body Is Begging You to Run More Trails Instead of Roads

items.title: New Research Analyzed 82 Studies to Find Out Whether Skiing or Snowboarding Is Safer
items.summary:
Skiing and snowboarding both come with risks, and it’s difficult to say definitively if one is more dangerous than the other. But recent research suggests the answer may depend on your skill level.

The authors of the study, published in the journal Health Science Reports , found that snowboarding may be more dangerous at the professional level, while skiing may be more dangerous for amateurs.

The researchers also examined which types of injuries are most common among snowboarders and skiers. Their results offer insight into what snowboarders and skiers, particularly recreational skiers, can do to stay safe.

“As a primary care sports medicine physician, what stood out to me was how often a recreational injury started with an ordinary fall,” Sabrina Sawlani, DO , a primary care sports medicine physician, told Outside . Sawlani is an assistant clinical professor in the department of orthopedic surgery in the division of primary care sports medicine at UCLA Health in Los Angeles and was not involved in the study.

“The new research helps us tailor injury prevention advice to the sport and the kind of skiing or riding someone does,” she said.

Which Sport Is More Dangerous: Skiing or Snowboarding? 
 The researchers analyzed 82 studies that provided data on skiing and snowboarding injuries. Out of every 100,000 runs, professional alpine skiers reported two injuries; for pro snowboarders, that rate was much higher: 380 injuries per 100,000 runs. items.t: New Research Analyzed 82 Studies to Find Out Whether Skiing or Snowboarding Is Safer
